extracted.intended_audience: playwrights, dramatists, literary critics, and students of drama
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for writing, staging, and critically assessing dramatic works (characterization, plot probability, moral purpose, stagecraft, and language). Useful for playwrights and critics judging dramatic effectiveness and plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intellectual power as dramatic attraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Of all power, that of the mind is ... the grand desideratum of human ambition. We shall be as Gods in knowledge ... the coexistence of great intellectual lordship with guilt has never been adequately represented without exciting the strongest interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters who combine great intellect with moral guilt or conflict are intrinsically interesting; represent the intellect as sometimes a separate, self-subsistent force (rather than merely subordinated to conscience) to create strong dramatic interest (examples: Shakespeare’s Richard, Iago, Edmund).

rubrics_metrics.name: Superiority to fear of the invisible world
rubrics_metrics.description: Of all intellectual power, that of superiority to the fear of the invisible world is the most dazzling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters who bravely defy the supernatural (or appear to) create a striking effect and can 'bribe' audiences into suspending judgment; use such superiority to heighten interest (Don John before his father’s ghost is given as an example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatic probability via harmony of the whole
rubrics_metrics.description: A specific dramatic probability may be raised by a true poet, if the whole of his work be in harmony: a dramatic probability, sufficient for dramatic pleasure, even when the component characters and incidents border on impossibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You need not make every incident literally probable; ensure internal harmony and consistent tone across the work so audiences will 'yield themselves to a dream' rather than demand literal belief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Solicit a dream, not belief
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet does not require us to be awake and believe; he solicits us only to yield ourselves to a dream; and this too with our eyes open, and with our judgment perdue behind the curtain, ready to awaken us at the first motion of our will: and meantime, only, not to disbelieve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask the audience for willing suspension of disbelief — maintain enough internal coherence that their judgment can be safely kept 'behind the curtain' until they choose to reapply it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground supernatural effects or risk gratuitousness
rubrics_metrics.description: But what is there to account for the prodigy of the tempest ... It is a mere supernatural effect, without even a hint of any supernatural agency; a prodigy, without any circumstance mentioned that is prodigious; and a miracle introduced without a ground, and ending without a result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If introducing prodigies/miracles or extreme supernatural storms, provide a hinted agency, causal groundwork, or lasting consequence; otherwise the effect reads as scene-for-scene spectacle with no dramatic justification (Bertram’s shipwreck is given as a counterexample).

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral purpose and the critique of hollow virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Nor is the scene ... susceptible likewise of a sound moral; ... the Atheista Fulminato presents an exquisite portraiture of the same qualities, in all their gloss and glow, but presents them for the sole purpose of displaying their hollowness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A play gains depth when it uses character qualities (e.g., honour, courage) not merely as ornaments but to demonstrate their moral value or hollowness; avoid presenting 'gentlemanly' qualities as substitutes for real virtue without showing their consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid rewarding criminals by misplaced sympathy
rubrics_metrics.description: The whole secret of the modern jacobinical drama ... consists in the confusion and subversion of the natural order of things ... rewarding with all the sympathies which are the due of virtue, those criminals whom law, reason, and religion have excommunicated from our esteem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious about portraying criminal characters with the trappings of virtue in ways that elicit undeserved sympathy — examine whether you are subverting moral order merely for surprise or sentimental effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency of character action and role
rubrics_metrics.description: The Prior ... knew, and confesses that he knew, that Bertram’s 'fearful mates' were assassins ... To the Castle however he goes, thus with the holy Prior’s consent, if not with his assistance; ... the Prior’s consent but no effective action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure characters' actions follow from their knowledge and role. If a character is angry, alarmed, or claims to know danger, their behavior should include plausible responses (not merely scolding or passive behavior) unless a deliberate and justified counterintuitive motive is shown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid contrivance and convenient plotting
rubrics_metrics.description: A convenient fainting fit ... just in time to give Bertram an opportunity ... a most convenient fainting fit of our lady’s, just in time to give Bertram an opportunity of seeking the object of his hatred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on artificially-timed faints, knockings, arrivals, or other stage conveniences to advance plot; contrived devices weaken credibility and audience trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportional blending of traits to prevent flatness
rubrics_metrics.description: The character of Don John consists in the union of every thing desirable to human nature, as means ... more especially in that constant interpoise of wit, gaiety, and social generosity, which prevents the criminal, even in his most atrocious moments, from sinking into the mere ruffian.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Complex characters should mix traits (wit, generosity, gaiety) in balanced proportion so that villainy does not flatten into mere caricature; use contrasts to sustain interest and imagination’s judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language quality: diction and metre matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Though crowded with solecisms, corrupt diction, and offences against metre, would possess merits sufficient to out-weigh them, if we could suspend the moral sense during the perusal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid solecisms and corrupt diction and be attentive to metre where relevant. Strong emotional or structural merits can sometimes outweigh technical lapses, but be aware they erode craft credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid sensationalism as cheap crowd-pleasing
rubrics_metrics.description: The shocking spirit of jacobinism seemed no longer confined to politics ... craving alone for the grossest and most outrageous stimulants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not pander to audiences with gratuitous horror, profanity, or shocking scenes simply to elicit applause; such sensationalism can indicate a depravation of civic taste and cheapen the work’s moral and aesthetic aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Originality and coherence of imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: Observe too these images stand unique in the speeches of Imogine, without the slightest resemblance to anything she says before or after.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure imagery and metaphors flow naturally from a character’s established voice; isolated or plagiarized images that do not cohere with prior speech break verisimilitude and feel jarring.

rubrics_metrics.name: Justify sudden reversals in character
rubrics_metrics.description: The steady, quiet uprightness of the flame ... the Prior’s last scene ... with a most surprising revolution, he whines, weeps, and kneels ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a character undergoes a dramatic temperament reversal (e.g., scolding to sobbing devotion), provide believable causes or gradual development; unexplained revolutions appear 'outre' and prompt audience suspicion that the change is contrived.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolve major plot threads clearly
rubrics_metrics.description: She had, it appears, taken her child with her, but what becomes of the child, whether she murdered it or not, nobody can tell ... it was a riddle at the representation, and after a most attentive perusal of the Play, a riddle it remains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not leave central narrative facts (the fate of a child, the consequence of a major action) unresolved or inscrutable without deliberate thematic purpose; ambiguity should be purposeful, not the result of negligence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain decorum in stage representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Of the fifth act, the only thing noticeable ... is the profane representation of the high altar in a chapel, with all the vessels and other preparations for the holy sacrament. A hymn is actually sung on the stage by the chorister boys!
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be careful with staging sacred objects/rites or blending solemn religious elements with profane or sensational content; mishandling sacred imagery can feel profane and alienate audience sensibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handle backstory and retrospective narration effectively
rubrics_metrics.description: This, notwithstanding, is the best scene in the Play ... It tells well and passionately the preliminary circumstances, and thus overcomes the main difficulty of most first acts, to wit, that of retrospective narration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a first act must convey past events, do so vividly and passionately to avoid cumbersome exposition; good handling of backstory overcomes typical first-act weaknesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid vague, stock physical descriptions and clichés
rubrics_metrics.description: He attracts the notice ... by his 'wild and terrible dark eyes,' 'muffled form,' 'fearful form,' 'darkly wild,' 'proudly stern,' and the like common-place indefinites, seasoned by merely verbal antitheses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor precise, character-revealing description over commonplace adjectival clichés; avoid piling stock epithets that reduce a figure to a theatrical silhouette rather than a living person.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderate exaggerated physical acting/stage effects
rubrics_metrics.description: The dramatic effect of which passage we not only concede ... but acknowledge the further advantages of preparing the audience for the most surprising series of wry faces, proflated mouths, and lunatic gestures that were ever 'launched' on an audience to 'sear the sense.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exaggerated contortions, overblown lunatic gestures, or perpetual 'startling' faces undermine credibility and can desensitize an audience; use physicality purposefully and sparingly to preserve impact.
